title: Body Language

jokes.text: Michael insists the office speak only Spanish, greeting everyone as 'Miguel'
jokes.setup: Michael greets Erin cheerfully in Spanish and establishes a 'Spanish only' rule
jokes.punchline: The rule is revealed to be entirely self-serving — he's going to Cancun next week
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael Scott structure: he frames a self-indulgent whim as altruistic and grand. The 'healing for all of North America' pivot to 'I'm going to Cancun' is well-timed and deeply character-specific. Medium-strength opener.

jokes.text: Jim talking head: 'Michael's relationship with the English language has always been at best, tenuous, and at worst, abusive. So it's nice to see him with a language that makes him happy and brief.'
jokes.setup: Jim observes Michael's Spanish-only initiative
jokes.punchline: 'Brief' — the killer final word doing double duty: Spanish vocabulary is brief AND Michael's competence keeps his sentences short
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Tenuous... abusive' is already strong, but 'brief' is perfectly placed — it's funny on the surface (Spanish is briefer for Michael) and devastating as a commentary on Michael's verbal incontinence. Maximum economy. The word 'brief' carries enormous comedic payload for one syllable.

jokes.text: Dwight talking head: 'I have it on very good authority that within 20 years, everyone will be speaking German. Or a Chinese-German hybrid.'
jokes.setup: Dwight dismisses Michael's Spanish initiative
jokes.punchline: 'Or a Chinese-German hybrid' — the escalation into an absurd geopolitical linguistic prediction delivered with total conviction
jokes.explanation: Pure Dwight — confident, authoritative, completely deranged. 'Or a Chinese-German hybrid' is the right escalation: specific enough to be absurd, delivered without irony. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Michael labels objects with genital drawings to remember grammatical gender in Spanish
jokes.setup: Jim suggests Michael mark everything with 'the international symbol for gender' to help with masculine/feminine nouns
jokes.punchline: Jim's talking head: 'I should have been more specific. Your office is full of genitalia.'
jokes.explanation: Strong visual comedy enhanced by the mockumentary format — the punchline is Jim's deadpan confession to camera. The structure is excellent: Jim creates the problem, Jim reveals the consequence. 'Your office is full of genitalia' is a wonderful sentence.

jokes.text: Michael says 'Eso es lo que dice él' — 'That's what he says' — accidentally doing a Spanish 'That's what she said'
jokes.setup: Michael uses his new Spanish phrase and Jim translates it
jokes.punchline: Jim: 'That's what HE says?' Michael: 'Damn it.' — Michael has accidentally executed a gender-swapped version of his signature catchphrase in Spanish
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. It works on multiple levels simultaneously: the Spanish gender subplot pays off, Michael's most famous character trait is inverted, and his 'Damn it' shows genuine disappointment at botching his own catchphrase. The setup (gender in Spanish is hard for Michael) perfectly seeds the punchline. This is among the episode's best — highly character-specific, earned, and deeply satisfying for anyone who knows the show.

jokes.text: Michael calls Angela 'Angelo' and she corrects him flatly; he responds 'Yo soy Cancun'
jokes.setup: Michael greets Angela in his Spanish mode
jokes.punchline: 'Yo soy Cancun' — Michael's Spanish is so broken he has declared himself to be a city
jokes.explanation: Quick and efficient. 'Yo soy Cancun' is a delightful non-sequitur that caps the Spanish cold open nicely. The Angela correction beat is a good straight-man moment. Solid mid-tier joke.

jokes.text: Ryan and an unnamed person discussing cables: 'It's not a good idea to force it if the shapes don't match up.' / 'The shapes don't matter, Ryan. As long as there's a connection, stuff can pass through it.'
jokes.setup: Two people appear to be having a technical/sexual innuendo conversation about cables
jokes.punchline: The immediate cut to Michael's talking head about Donna, a woman he's attracted to — the cable conversation was innocent, but positioned as a double entendre given context
jokes.explanation: A mild double-entendre through juxtaposition. The joke is competent but not particularly sharp — the innuendo is slightly forced and the payoff relies on the cut rather than the lines themselves. Functional comedy.

jokes.text: Michael talking head about Donna: 'We're in the midst of a passionate love affair.' Cut to: 'Um, no. But she is coming by today maybe to buy some printers.'
jokes.setup: Michael sets up what sounds like a genuine romantic relationship
jokes.punchline: His immediate self-correction reveals it's entirely fabricated — she's just a potential printer customer
jokes.explanation: Well-structured misdirection that efficiently establishes the episode's A-plot and Michael's delusional romantic perception. The 'Um, no.' self-correction is perfectly timed. Good use of the talking-head format.

jokes.text: Jim tries to suggest a joke for the pitch: 'I just delivered a baby. They didn't offer me a guarantee.' Pam and Jim's shared cringe.
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are preparing a professional sales pitch together
jokes.punchline: Jim suggests a terrible joke, Pam immediately shuts it down — but the joke is so bad it's funny that Jim even floated it
jokes.explanation: A meta-joke about bad jokes. Jim suggesting a bad joke and Pam killing it is a nice couples moment, but the joke itself isn't strong enough to be funny as a bad joke. Competent filler.

jokes.text: Michael's joke pitch: 'I just delivered a baby. They didn't offer me a guarantee.' Jim's flat response: 'Yeah, or maybe we don't even need that.'
jokes.setup: Michael suggests adding a joke about delivery guarantees to the sales pitch
jokes.punchline: Jim's dismissal is funnier than the joke itself — the meta-comedy of a bad joke being rejected in real time
jokes.explanation: The joke-within-a-joke structure works — Michael's bad joke attempt is funny, Jim's deadpan dismissal is funnier. Good use of the Jim/Michael dynamic.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head: 'Can you smell the power of Halperts? Power couple. Mighty Morphin Power Rangers.' Andy: 'Oh, they wish they were Power Rangers. Good luck getting Ninjor to share his power coins with these two.' Kevin: 'Okay, nerd alert. Never saw the show. And that stuff was not in the movie.'
jokes.setup: The office reacts to Jim and Pam being assigned the joint sales pitch
jokes.punchline: Andy and Dwight's Power Rangers debate escalates into genuine nerd specificity — Kevin dismissing them both as nerds while clearly having seen only the movie is the cap
jokes.explanation: Solid ensemble joke. The escalating Power Rangers debate is funny because of its specificity (Ninjor, power coins), and Kevin's dismissal while revealing he only saw the movie is the best beat. Good character comedy.

jokes.text: Dwight on why Jim and Pam are bad choices: 'If you want people to put the best face on something, why would you get two people who probably have never cut the face off of anything in their lives?'
jokes.setup: Dwight argues he should get the client instead of Jim and Pam
jokes.punchline: Dwight's argument for 'putting the best face on' something involves face-removal, implying his experience with facial violence as a credential
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Dwight line. The idiom 'put the best face on something' is literalized in a horrifying direction that is entirely consistent with Dwight's survivalist, violent worldview. The phrase 'probably have never cut the face off of anything in their lives' is perfectly constructed — the 'probably' is the cherry on top. Could only come from Dwight. Strong candidate for best line of the episode.

jokes.text: Pam talking head: 'We have good give and take. I give, he takes!'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam describe their partnership as complementary
jokes.punchline: Pam's talking head flips it — 'I give, he takes' — undercutting Jim's self-satisfied description
jokes.explanation: A functional gag on marriage dynamics. The economy is strong but the joke is fairly predictable — you can see it coming once 'give and take' is mentioned. Pam's delivery would sell it more than the writing itself.

jokes.text: Jim's reaction face to camera after Pam says 'I give, he takes'
jokes.setup: Pam has just undercut Jim's description of their partnership
jokes.punchline: Jim's bewildered 'I don't even know who you are anymore' to camera — a classic Jim look elevated by his genuine surprise at Pam
jokes.explanation: A reliable Jim-to-camera beat. 'I don't even know who you are anymore' is mildly funny but the real laugh is in his expression. Solid use of the format.

jokes.text: Michael introduces Donna to the office: 'Did somebody order a hooker over here?'
jokes.setup: Michael is greeting an attractive woman at the office he's trying to impress
jokes.punchline: Michael's idea of a charming greeting is calling her a hooker — his complete lack of social awareness on full display
jokes.explanation: Peak Michael Scott greeting — simultaneously a compliment and an insult, delivered with confidence. The cringe lands because Donna handles it well, which makes Michael seem even more oblivious. Familiar territory but executed cleanly.

jokes.text: Michael tells Donna that Jim and Pam 'look exactly alike' and when Donna says she has a sense about these things and they probably 'have ancestors in common somewhere back,' Michael says 'I knew it.'
jokes.setup: Michael introduces Jim and Pam as the 'Wonder Twins.' Donna says they look alike.
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately agrees with Donna's insinuation that Jim and Pam might be distantly related — 'I knew it' — betraying zero loyalty to the couple he's supposedly championing
jokes.explanation: Good cringe sequence — the escalation from 'you look alike' to implied incest is handled with a light touch. Michael's 'I knew it' is the best beat, showing his eagerness to agree with anything the pretty woman says.

jokes.text: Michael on Donna's restaurant visit: 'Dined and dashed. Usually they don't follow you to your place of work. Happens sometimes. Part of the game.'
jokes.setup: Michael tries to cover for not remembering what people drink at Donna's restaurant
jokes.punchline: He casually admits they dine and dashed — and frames it as a normal, philosophically acceptable practice
jokes.explanation: 'Part of the game' is a great line — Michael has a worldview where dine-and-dashing is just sports. The casual delivery makes it funnier. Solid Michael moment.

jokes.text: Michael interrupts the sales pitch to ask Donna if she shops at Victoria's Secret, claiming magazines are being sent to his condo address for a previous tenant — Pam points out: 'None of this is time sensitive.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are making a professional sales pitch to Donna
jokes.punchline: Michael bursts in with a convoluted, obviously fake excuse to talk to Donna about lingerie catalogs — Pam flatly notes 'None of this is time sensitive'
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of Michael's excuse (Victoria's Secret magazines, previous tenant, sale through May) is great cringe comedy. Pam's deadpan 'None of this is time sensitive' is the perfect punctuation.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'Do I realize Donna's an attractive person? Yes. Am I attracted to her? Yes. Does that mean I am more excited to sell her printers than to someone else, some ugly client? Yes.'
jokes.setup: Michael rationalizes his disruptive behavior during the sales pitch
jokes.punchline: 'Some ugly client' — Michael's logic concludes with cheerful confirmation of bias, framing appearance-based favoritism as entirely reasonable
jokes.explanation: The rhetorical triple-question structure works well, and 'some ugly client' is the key phrase — Michael's honesty about shallow priorities is his most consistently funny trait. Good but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Donna's reaction to the Sabre 'Print in All Colors' minority executive program: 'Doesn't just sound a'ight, it sounds amazing.' Michael corrects: 'I didn't say a'ight.'
jokes.setup: Michael reads out the program details with corporate enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: Donna catches Michael unconsciously code-switching — he said 'a'ight' without realizing it, then denies it
jokes.explanation: Sharp observational joke about Michael's racial awkwardness — he code-switches unconsciously when pitching to Darryl (who is Black) and gets caught. The denial is perfect. Good social comedy.

jokes.text: Michael on Darryl potentially being in the program: 'Ten seconds ago, this guy was driving a forklift. Okay? Now, all of a sudden, he's Cinderella of the office.'
jokes.setup: Darryl expresses interest in the minority executive training program
jokes.punchline: Michael's incredulity — and his choice of 'Cinderella' — reveals his inability to imagine Darryl as executive material despite championing the program
jokes.explanation: 'Cinderella of the office' is a great phrase — Michael accidentally reveals his condescension while ostensibly promoting opportunity. The irony is rich and character-specific.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head choosing between Darryl and Kelly: 'The competent, hardworking one who does things his own way, or the malleable simpleton who can be bought for a few fashion magazines?'
jokes.setup: Michael considers which minority employee to back for the program
jokes.punchline: He describes Kelly as a 'malleable simpleton who can be bought for a few fashion magazines' — choosing her because she's easier to control, not because she deserves it
jokes.explanation: 'Malleable simpleton who can be bought for a few fashion magazines' is a wonderfully specific and accurate description of Kelly as Michael sees her. The implicit admission that he prefers easily-managed employees is a good character beat.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head choosing between Darryl and Kelly for the program: 'The competent, hardworking one who does things his own way, or the malleable simpleton who can be bought for a few fashion magazines?'
jokes.setup: Michael must decide which minority employee to recommend for the executive program
jokes.punchline: He frames the choice in terms of who he can manipulate — the 'malleable simpleton' who can 'be bought for fashion magazines' is his preferred candidate
jokes.explanation: Sharp dark comedy about Michael's managerial priorities — he explicitly favors incompetence because it's easier to control. 'Bought for a few fashion magazines' is a great specific detail. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Phone call scene: customer service rep says 'White people, right?' — Michael enthusiastically agrees, then the rep notes maybe the angry customer wasn't white. Michael: 'Well, you can kind of tell from the voice.'
jokes.setup: An angry phone customer yells about clothing sizes
jokes.punchline: Michael's attempt to bond racially with Darryl by agreeing 'White people, right?' immediately falls apart when Darryl questions the assumption — Michael doubles down with 'you can kind of tell from the voice'
jokes.explanation: Good cringe comedy about Michael's racial cluelessness. The 'you can kind of tell from the voice' line is the perfect Michael Scott escalation — he doubles down on something already awkward.

jokes.text: Michael tells Darryl he probably gets pulled over for his race; Darryl says they say it's because of texting. Then Michael tells him he's probably paid less — Darryl makes $17/hour for phone calls. Michael: 'A goat with a tape recorder could—'
jokes.setup: Michael tries to build solidarity with Darryl by listing racist injustices Darryl must face
jokes.punchline: Darryl keeps dismantling Michael's assumptions — and Michael's response to learning Darryl earns $17/hour is to insult the job rather than revise his worldview
jokes.explanation: Escalating cringe that works well. Each of Michael's 'sympathetic' statements gets deflated, and 'a goat with a tape recorder' is a genuinely funny line that shows Michael's empathy has completely collapsed into insult territory. The cut mid-sentence adds to the joke.

jokes.text: Michael: 'You could be the Indian Bill Gates. You could be the Indian Ted Turner.' Kelly: 'I could be the Indian Julia Roberts.' Michael: 'That's not— She's— Okay. Yes.'
jokes.setup: Michael tries to inspire Kelly with examples of Indian success
jokes.punchline: Kelly's 'Indian Julia Roberts' breaks Michael's frame (he's listing business moguls) — and his defeated 'Okay. Yes.' is the surrender of a man who's given up correcting her
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-specific joke. 'Indian Julia Roberts' is perfectly Kelly — she pivots from business to celebrity entirely logically from her perspective. Michael's stuttering capitulation ('That's not— She's— Okay. Yes.') is as funny as the line itself. Strong integration of both characters.

jokes.text: Michael's sales technique: showing Donna photos of himself on the printer to make her associate him with things that 'turn her on' — 'Soon she doesn't know what is me, what is the image.'
jokes.setup: Michael demonstrates the printer's color quality with scanned self-portraits
jokes.punchline: His talking-head reveals this is a seduction strategy — Pavlovian conditioning via printed headshots
jokes.explanation: A great Michael delusion — the idea that he's devised a Pavlovian seduction scheme through printed photographs is wonderfully absurd. 'She doesn't know what is me, what is the image' is the kind of line that only Michael could deliver with complete sincerity.

jokes.text: Michael scanned a photo of himself in 'a place I like to go to be alone with my thoughts. I've never taken anybody there before.' — Jim: 'Who took the photo?' Michael: 'Ryan.'
jokes.setup: Michael describes his intimate private sanctuary as he shows Donna a romantic photo
jokes.punchline: If it's his secret private place and he's never taken anyone there, who took the photo? — Ryan did, instantly deflating the mystique
jokes.explanation: Tight, well-constructed joke. The setup creates a logical impossibility that Jim catches, and 'Ryan' as the answer is perfect — it both destroys the romance and implies Ryan was dragged to Michael's 'special place' for a photo shoot. Excellent economy.

jokes.text: Michael attempts to kiss Donna during the sales pitch — Jim is called in and comes to find Donna looking horrified
jokes.setup: Michael has been left alone with Donna while Jim goes to get materials
jokes.punchline: Jim returns to find chaos — Michael attempted to kiss Donna, treating his 'signals' misread as justification
jokes.explanation: The kiss attempt is a classic cringe escalation beat — the comedy is in the inevitability of it. The 'Jim called in' structure works well. High impact from the situation even if the individual writing isn't standout.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head after attempted kiss: 'It wouldn't have been inappropriate 50 years ago. "Mad Men."'
jokes.setup: Michael is asked if kissing a client at work was inappropriate
jokes.punchline: He invokes 'Mad Men' as a legal/moral defense — treating a TV show as historical precedent
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Mad Men' delivered as a one-word citation — as if it's a legal statute or historical document — is brilliant character comedy. It's incredibly quotable, deeply Michael, and the two-word drop lands like a complete thought. The economy is exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael: 'What about Pam? And you did a heck of a lot more than kiss.' Gesturing at Jim as justification for his own workplace kiss attempt.
jokes.setup: Jim tells Michael he shouldn't try to kiss people at work
jokes.punchline: Michael calls out Jim and Pam's relationship as precedent — 'you did a heck of a lot more than kiss' — using their romance to justify his harassment
jokes.explanation: Good use of show history — Michael weaponizes Jim and Pam's romance as a defense. Jim's inability to refute it is funny. 'A heck of a lot more than kiss' is a great Michael euphemism.

jokes.text: Donna's talking head: 'Was it professional? No. But I work in the nightlife industry. I get hit on all the time. In my 20s, it would have been annoying. In my late 20s, I find it really flattering.'
jokes.setup: Donna reacts to Michael's attempted kiss
jokes.punchline: Her rationale for not being upset is that being hit on in her 'late 20s' is flattering — the implication being she's slightly desperate or at least resigned
jokes.explanation: Good character reveal that does double duty — it's a joke about aging/dating expectations AND it moves the plot forward (explaining why Donna stays). The joke is funnier in retrospect when she actually kisses Michael at the end.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Team Shortbread!' — then the whole group devolves into competing Team Shortbread factions after Pam takes his side
jokes.setup: Michael offers shortbread to win support for going back to try with Donna; Pam takes one and agrees he should try again
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately declares 'Team Shortbread' as a political faction and tries to recruit members — the absurd formalization of biscuit-based alliance
jokes.explanation: A fun running bit that escalates appropriately. The joke works because Michael takes snack-based coalition building completely seriously. Pam's complicity is a good character moment.

jokes.text: Jim on Pam's soft support of Michael: 'Don't act like you understood anything that [the Schwab] guy said.'
jokes.setup: Jim invokes the Schwab investment advice guy to defend treating all sales seriously; Pam is dismissive
jokes.punchline: Jim's retort that Pam didn't understand the Schwab presentation either is a small but sharp couples-comedy beat
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient marital dig. Not a standout joke but it gets a genuine small laugh from its accuracy.

jokes.text: Michael talking head: 'Reading people's faces is an artform. A blind person can do it just by touch. A deaf person can do it by sight. A hearing and sighted person can do it, like me, by sight.'
jokes.setup: Michael explains his body language expertise before going back in to flirt with Donna
jokes.punchline: The speech builds through 'blind person... deaf person...' in a cadence that implies wisdom, then lands on the completely tautological 'a hearing and sighted person can do it, like me, by sight' — adding nothing
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best structured jokes. The tricolon setup mimics the form of inspirational wisdom ('blind... deaf... sighted person...') building anticipation, then the punchline is the total absence of the expected insight — 'like me, by sight.' It's a perfectly constructed anti-climax that rewards the rhythm. Strong originality.

jokes.text: Donna laughs at Michael's 'English Mike' accent bit: 'Oh my God, I thought you were from England just then. Do that again.' Michael: 'I'm English Mike.' Both delight in it.
jokes.setup: Michael accidentally slips into a British accent saying 'It twas the bus boy'
jokes.punchline: Donna is charmed — and Michael immediately commits to the bit with 'I'm English Mike. Yeah, baby! Yeah!' showing his appetite for any persona that gets attention
jokes.explanation: A cute, low-stakes moment. The 'English Mike' bit works because Michael's enthusiasm is contagious, but it's not a sharply written joke — it lives or dies on performance.

jokes.text: Michael talking head: 'We are tough, from the streets. Never took a handout. Always had to pull ourselves up from the boob straps.'
jokes.setup: Michael describes his kinship with Donna
jokes.punchline: 'Boob straps' — Michael's malapropism of 'bootstraps' that is simultaneously accidental and reveals exactly where his mind is
jokes.explanation: Exceptional. 'Boob straps' is a perfect Michael Scott malapropism — it's 'bootstraps' corrupted exactly as his subconscious (obsessed with Donna's appearance) would corrupt it. Two words that do everything: reveal his preoccupation, get a huge laugh, and work as a pure wordplay joke. Highly quotable. One of the episode's best individual jokes.

jokes.text: Dwight trying to coach Kelly: 'You have a terrible personality and an awful work ethic. Maybe we can cobble something together from the emotional turmoil you felt being an Indian.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is trying to help Kelly prepare her application for the minority executive program
jokes.punchline: Dwight's 'coaching' is just a string of insults culminating in pure racial instrumentalization — treating Kelly's ethnicity as the only usable asset she has
jokes.explanation: Solid Dwight/Kelly cringe comedy. The pivot from 'terrible personality and awful work ethic' to 'emotional turmoil of being Indian' as the plan is darkly funny. Strong Dwight voice.

jokes.text: Dwight berates Kelly about her 'accent': 'You do. Central Pennsylvania. Allentown suburbs, maybe. It's really annoying.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is coaching Kelly for her minority program interview
jokes.punchline: Dwight matter-of-factly diagnoses Kelly's 'annoying' central Pennsylvania accent — she doesn't have a foreign accent, she has a suburban American one
jokes.explanation: Dwight's complete confidence in his geographic accent analysis is funny. The joke is that he's been expecting an ethnic accent and Kelly just has a suburban American one — his deflation is the comedy.

jokes.text: Dwight on Kelly's accent: 'I'm sorry. It's just your accent. Sometimes that's all I can hear. The rest just sounds like gibberish.'
jokes.setup: Kelly shares something genuine about her experience ('everyone thinks I want to be a doctor')
jokes.punchline: Dwight confesses he can't hear anything past her accent — mid-coaching session
jokes.explanation: Good cringe. The audacity of Dwight admitting mid-coaching that he hasn't heard a word Kelly said because of her accent is both insulting and very in-character. 'The rest just sounds like gibberish' is a good specific line.

jokes.text: Kevin: 'You ever notice you can only ooze two things: sexuality and pus. Man, I tell ya.'
jokes.setup: Jim says 'Some people can't help oozing sexuality'
jokes.punchline: Kevin's pedantic correction that the only two things that can be oozed are sexuality and pus — delivered like a late-night comedian
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes, coming from an unexpected source. Kevin's 'Man, I tell ya' at the end positions him as a stand-up comic making a genuine observational point — and the observation itself (the limited vocabulary of 'ooze') is both gross and logically correct. Completely original, perfectly economical, and Kevin-specific in its guileless delivery. High quotability.

jokes.text: Andy talking head on reading signals: 'It's easier than it used to be. If a lady is interested, she'll send me a wink. And then I'll send back an e-flirt. And if it doesn't work out, I block her.'
jokes.setup: The group is discussing how to tell if someone is interested in you romantically
jokes.punchline: Andy describes his romantic life as entirely digital — winks, e-flirts, blocking — as if these are sophisticated techniques, ending with 'I block her' as a perfectly casual denouement
jokes.explanation: Good Andy character moment. 'I block her' as the unselfconscious conclusion to a dating strategy is very funny — it implies volume (he blocks many women) and a complete emotional non-involvement. Character-specific and well-paced.

jokes.text: Meredith talking head: 'She's way out of his league. It'd be like me going for Sean Hannity.'
jokes.setup: Meredith comments on Michael's chances with Donna
jokes.punchline: Her reference point for 'out of her league' is Sean Hannity — suggesting that's whom she would aim for, which reveals both her political leanings and her self-assessment
jokes.explanation: Unexpected and character-specific. Meredith's frame of reference for 'aspirational' being Sean Hannity is funny and says a lot about her in one line. A good quick joke that uses the format efficiently.

jokes.text: Oscar: 'There's a third base? Baseball? Really? I always thought it was based on orchestra chairs.' — pause — 'And now you're telling me there's a third base in the orchestra? No. That's a bass-heavy orchestra.'
jokes.setup: Kevin says Michael 'hasn't gotten to third base' yet; Oscar claims not to understand the baseball/romance metaphor
jokes.punchline: Oscar's extended confusion — playing the gay man who doesn't recognize heterosexual dating metaphors — culminates in the genuine pun: 'bass-heavy orchestra'
jokes.explanation: A layered joke. Oscar's 'I don't understand this metaphor' bit is good character comedy, but the real payoff is 'bass-heavy orchestra' — a genuine pun that Oscar seems to arrive at spontaneously. The extended working-out of the metaphor is slightly long but the landing is worth it.

jokes.text: Kevin, analyzing Donna's crossed arms: 'Maybe she's just pushing her breasts together to make them look bigger.' — then appears to demonstrate on himself
jokes.setup: The office is body-language-watching Michael through the glass; someone suggests crossed arms is a bad sign
jokes.punchline: Kevin's alternative explanation — and his apparent physical demonstration — is completely Kevin: simultaneously crass, cheerful, and offering it as genuine analysis
jokes.explanation: The visual of Kevin demonstrating breast-pushing on himself elevates what would otherwise be a mediocre line. Physical comedy via implication is strong here. Kevin's earnestness makes it work.

jokes.text: Jim on selling at a loss: 'Sometimes it makes financial sense to lose money, right? Like for tax purposes.' Ryan: 'Actually, ran the numbers on this, and in this case it makes more financial sense to gain money.'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to justify giving Donna a steep discount because Michael is flirting
jokes.punchline: Ryan's 'it makes more financial sense to gain money' is profoundly obvious stated as if it's a sophisticated analysis — delivered completely straight
jokes.explanation: A great deadpan joke. 'It makes more financial sense to gain money' is simultaneously the most obvious and most useless thing anyone could say — and Ryan delivers it as if he's done serious analysis. The economy is excellent. Highly quotable in context.

jokes.text: Michael's tip to test Donna's interest: 'Ask her if she wants a mint. If she says no, then she is not interested.' — and then Michael actually does this, and Donna says yes
jokes.setup: The group devises a test for whether Donna likes Michael
jokes.punchline: The mint test is an absurd pseudo-scientific method that Michael takes completely literally — and Donna accepts the mint, which Michael treats as conclusive evidence
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist bit. The mint as romantic litmus test is ridiculous, and the callback of Michael actually deploying it adds comedic mileage. The mint-acceptance becoming conclusive proof is very Michael.

jokes.text: Pam: 'You can flirt with someone to get what you want and also be attracted to them. How do you think we got together?' Jim: ''Cause I stopped by your desk like 15 times a day.' Pam: 'I was after your money.' Jim: 'Well, the joke was on you.' Pam: 'Yes, it was.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam debate whether Donna is flirting with Michael or genuinely interested
jokes.punchline: Their own origin story becomes the example — Pam claims she was 'after Jim's money,' Jim's retort ('the joke was on you') and Pam's agreement ('yes, it was') confirms he had no money
jokes.explanation: A warm, well-constructed exchange. The turn on 'the joke was on you' followed by Pam's sincere 'yes, it was' is a small masterpiece of married comedy — affectionate and deflating simultaneously. Strong couple-specific writing.

jokes.text: Michael to Gabe about Indian CEOs: 'Soft drink ain't paper, Gabe. Now name one significant paper company CEO that's Indian. Just one, and I'm out of your hair. Name two.'
jokes.setup: Gabe lists several prominent Indian CEOs to counter Michael's claim that Kelly has no Indian role models
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately narrows the criteria to 'paper company CEOs' — and then immediately asks for two instead of one
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. Michael's goalpost-moving from 'any CEO' to 'paper company CEO' is already funny, but 'name two' immediately after promising 'I'm out of your hair' after one is a perfect escalation. The logic is pure Michael — self-serving and oblivious. Strong structure.

jokes.text: Kelly and Ryan cyberbully a girl from the mall. Ryan: 'Tell her everyone in homeroom thinks she's fat.' Kelly: 'Oh, that is so good.'
jokes.setup: Kelly is angry at a girl who was rude to her at the mall
jokes.punchline: Kelly and Ryan's solution is to create a fake account to make a teenager anorexic — Ryan's enthusiastic contribution and Kelly's delight in it reveals their shared moral bankruptcy
jokes.explanation: Dark comedy that works because of character — Kelly's pettiness and Ryan's eager collaboration are completely in-character. The specificity of 'trying to make her anorexic' as the stated goal is darkly funny. Aged slightly given real-world context but the character work is sharp.

jokes.text: Kelly on interview prep: 'It's easy. You just turn every question around on them.' Practice: 'Do you think you're treated differently because of your race?' Kelly: 'Would you ask that same question if I was white?' Kelly/Ryan: 'We're so in.'
jokes.setup: Ryan coaches Kelly on interview technique
jokes.punchline: The technique of turning every question around is demonstrated perfectly — Kelly's response to a race question is itself a race-based deflection — and both celebrate prematurely
jokes.explanation: Sharp joke. The interview technique actually works in this case — 'would you ask that same question if I was white?' is a legitimately good deflection — which makes Ryan and Kelly's confidence both absurd and weirdly warranted. The 'we're so in' said in unison is a great button.

jokes.text: Dwight talking head: 'If you'd have told me this morning that today I'd be creating a monster capable of my own destruction, I'd have thought you were referring to the bull Mose and I are trying to reanimate.'
jokes.setup: Dwight realizes Kelly, now empowered, could be worse for him than Darryl
jokes.punchline: His frame of reference for 'monster capable of my own destruction' is the reanimated bull he and Mose are working on — delivered as a completely casual aside
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Dwight joke. 'The bull Mose and I are trying to reanimate' is thrown away as a subordinate clause — a throwaway detail that implies an entire off-screen horror subplot involving Dwight and his cousin reanimating livestock. The casual specificity ('the bull') suggests this is an ongoing project. One of the episode's best jokes. Perfect character integration — could only be Dwight.

jokes.text: Michael talking head: 'Her words are telling me to back off. But her eyes, and her smile, and her overall vibe is telling me to go for it. And I just think it's unfair that our society puts more weight on words than on somebody's vibe.'
jokes.setup: Donna has explicitly told Michael to back off
jokes.punchline: Michael's philosophical complaint — that words are unfairly privileged over 'vibe' as communication — is a self-serving rationalization dressed as social commentary
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's thematic jokes — it literalizes the episode title ('Body Language') through Michael's worldview. The delivery of a genuine philosophical complaint about consent communication is darkly comic and entirely character-specific. 'More weight on words than on somebody's vibe' is a memorable, quotable line.

jokes.text: Michael rushes back in and tries to kiss Donna a second time; Jim has to physically restrain him.
jokes.setup: The whole office watches Michael try the mint test, then he escalates to another kiss attempt
jokes.punchline: Michael can't stop himself — 'I can't stop myself from kissing her' — treated as a force of nature rather than a choice
jokes.explanation: The physical escalation is funny as cringe payoff but the writing doesn't do much work here — the comedy is situational. Jim's 'Yeah, now you know how I feel sitting next to those M&Ms all day' is the best line in the beat.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I can't stop myself from kissing her.' Jim: 'Yeah, now you know how I feel sitting next to those M&Ms all day.' Michael: 'Well, why don't you just move the M&Ms?' Jim: 'Well, why don't you shut up!'
jokes.setup: Michael explains he can't control his impulse to kiss Donna
jokes.punchline: Jim uses M&Ms as his parallel — and when Michael logically suggests moving them, Jim has no defense and snaps 'Why don't you shut up!'
jokes.explanation: Excellent exchange. Jim's M&M parallel is funny, but Michael's logical rebuttal ('why don't you just move the M&Ms?') completely defeats Jim's analogy, forcing him into the indefensible 'Well, why don't you shut up!' The reversal — Jim losing a logic argument to Michael — is a great comedic beat and subverts their usual dynamic.

jokes.text: Michael: 'What sort of movie would Rudy have been if he had just stopped, given up, after two rejections? Would have been a lot shorter. Probably been a lot funnier. But it would have ultimately been a disappointment. I still would have seen it. But that's not... the point.'
jokes.setup: Michael invokes 'Rudy' as inspirational precedent for not giving up on Donna
jokes.punchline: Michael's analysis of alternate-Rudy — 'probably been a lot funnier... I still would have seen it' — undermines his own argument while somehow maintaining conviction
jokes.explanation: A standout speech. Michael's Rudy argument collapses in real-time: 'probably been a lot funnier' is an honest concession that a shorter Rudy might have been better, and 'I still would have seen it' acknowledges the movie is good regardless of his point. 'But that's not... the point' — said with the pause of someone who has lost track of their own point — is perfect. This is the episode's best Michael monologue.

jokes.text: Dwight argues Kelly is disqualified because 'anthropologically, she is Indian. Indians migrated from the Caucuses region of Europe. Therefore, technically, she is Caucasian. You're welcome, America.'
jokes.setup: Dwight tries to disqualify Kelly from the minority program to give Darryl a better shot
jokes.punchline: 'You're welcome, America' — Dwight's self-congratulation for deploying pseudoscientific anthropology to deny someone minority status
jokes.explanation: Solid Dwight absurdism. The pseudo-historical argument is exactly the kind of thing Dwight would research and deploy with complete confidence. 'You're welcome, America' as the sign-off is the perfect button — Dwight's patriotism weaponized for petty office politics.

jokes.text: Darryl: 'I got my whole life to be a minority executive. I only have about a year left in these knees, though.'
jokes.setup: Darryl explains why he withdrew his application to the program
jokes.punchline: He's prioritizing his softball league over a Yale executive program because his knees won't last — delivered with complete pragmatic calm
jokes.explanation: Excellent Darryl line. The ratio of 'whole life to be a minority executive' vs. 'about a year left in these knees' perfectly captures Darryl's hierarchy of values — and it's absolutely character-specific. The deadpan practicality is the joke. Very quotable. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Michael sees the bindi on Angela's forehead: 'That's very nice. I never noticed that before.' Angela: 'Sometimes my bangs cover it.' Michael: 'Yeah. I don't want to be offensive but, uh, may I ask you what that means?' Angela: 'I do find that offensive, actually.'
jokes.setup: Michael, desperate to find a minority candidate, notices Angela's forehead
jokes.punchline: Angela is wearing a bindi — but she's not Indian, she's just Angela — and she finds Michael's inquiry offensive anyway
jokes.explanation: Good cringe. The joke works because Angela's 'I do find that offensive, actually' — where the offense is at the question itself, not at being mistaken for Indian — is a perfect Angela reaction. The setup pays off on her uptightness rather than Michael's racism.

jokes.text: Michael returns from the parking lot: 'Okay, finally. That bartender would not leave.'
jokes.setup: The whole office waits to hear what happened with Donna
jokes.punchline: Michael's first words home are a complaint about a bartender — implying he got rejected and went directly to a bar, which he doesn't even acknowledge
jokes.explanation: Nice understated joke. The implication that Michael immediately went to a bar after another rejection — told sideways through the bartender complaint — is sad and funny and very Michael. Good economy of storytelling.

jokes.text: Dwight recruits minorities: 'How would one of you feel if I told you I could put you on a fast track to an executive position?' Kevin: 'Holy cow. I'd be so happy.' Dwight: 'I wasn't talking to you, Pale Face.'  Kevin: 'I know. I meant I'd be happy for them.'
jokes.setup: Dwight tries to recruit minority employees for the program
jokes.punchline: Kevin's enthusiasm followed by Dwight's 'Pale Face' rejection — then Kevin's pivot to 'I meant I'd be happy for them' is so fast and sincere it implies he truly was just excited on others' behalf
jokes.explanation: Good quick joke. 'Pale Face' is an unexpectedly blunt Dwight choice, and Kevin's sincere pivot is sweet and funny. The exchange is efficient.

jokes.text: Dwight to Oscar: 'Speaking of rainbows, Oscar... you are kind of a double minority. Gay.' — then immediately pivots away without explaining the rainbow connection
jokes.setup: Dwight is recruiting minorities; someone references rainbows in the program title
jokes.punchline: Dwight pivots to Oscar as a 'double minority' — the rainbow-gay connection hanging unexplained — and 'Gay.' as a standalone sentence is the punchline
jokes.explanation: Good use of Dwight's bluntness. 'Gay.' as a declarative standalone sentence after 'Speaking of rainbows' is funny — Dwight making the gay=rainbow connection without acknowledging it. The 'double minority' framing is classic Dwight utility-thinking.

jokes.text: Oscar and the other minorities refuse to apply, not because the program isn't good, but because they're scared of Kelly. Dwight: 'Are we scared of Kelly? That's ridiculous.' Cut to everyone clearly being scared of Kelly.
jokes.setup: Dwight tries to get minorities to apply despite Kelly already having applied
jokes.punchline: The entire office is too scared of Kelly's retaliation to apply — and Dwight's 'That's ridiculous' is undercut by everyone's body language confirming they are indeed scared
jokes.explanation: Good ensemble joke that pays off Kelly's established terrifying energy. The fear being real and justified — for Kelly — is funny character work. The 'we're not scared' / clearly scared structure is reliable but well-executed.

jokes.text: Kelly's interview application 'hobbies': yoga, belly dancing, snake charming, beds of nails.
jokes.setup: Kelly is listing hobbies for her executive program application
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from yoga (plausible) to belly dancing (Indian stereotype) to snake charming (absurd stereotype) to 'beds of nails, I like lying on them' — each more outrageous
jokes.explanation: Good Kelly joke. The escalation from realistic to stereotyped to surreal is well-constructed. 'Beds of nails, I like lying on them' as a genuine hobby added as a casual afterthought is the best part. Kelly's lack of self-awareness about the stereotypes she's perpetuating is key to the joke.

jokes.text: Dwight bursts in with Hidetoshi for the program. Michael: 'Dwight, what are you doing?' Dwight: 'Helping heal America in a dramatic fashion in the 11th hour.'
jokes.setup: The program application deadline is near; Dwight has been trying to find a minority candidate
jokes.punchline: 'Helping heal America in a dramatic fashion in the 11th hour' — Dwight's grandiose description of recruiting a warehouse worker to a corporate training program
jokes.explanation: Solid Dwight line. His self-heroizing framing — 'heal America' and 'dramatic fashion' — for what is a mundane and self-serving act is very in-character and gets a good laugh.

jokes.text: Dwight's ranked list of who he tried before Hidetoshi: 'My first choice was Oscar, then Stanley, then Calvin, Danny, Alfonso, Hassan, Tad, Diego, Greg P., Greg M., Demetrious, and Hank the Security Guard.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks why Dwight chose Hidetoshi
jokes.punchline: Dwight has a ranked list of 13 people he approached before getting to Hidetoshi — the list is enormous, and it includes 'Greg P., Greg M.' (distinctions suggesting he knows multiple Gregs well enough to rank them) and Hank the Security Guard at the bottom
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the specificity and length of the list — it implies Dwight had detailed rejection conversations with 13 people before settling on Hidetoshi. 'Greg P., Greg M.' and 'Hank the Security Guard' are the standout details. The exhaustiveness is funny because it suggests Hidetoshi was truly the last resort.

jokes.text: Kelly: 'God, I hate you so much!' Dwight: 'Caucasians, am I right?'
jokes.setup: Kelly is furious that Dwight is trying to bring in competition for her spot
jokes.punchline: Dwight's response to Kelly's anger is to commiserate with Hidetoshi against white people — 'Caucasians, am I right?' — despite being as Caucasian as possible
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. Dwight attempting to bond with Hidetoshi by complaining about Caucasians — while being the most Caucasian man in the building — is peak Dwight social obliviousness. 'Caucasians, am I right?' is perfectly economical and highly quotable. Strong economy.

jokes.text: Dwight immediately tries to 'translate' for Hidetoshi, who doesn't need it: 'Why? I don't need translator.' Dwight: 'You don't know what you need. Just...'
jokes.setup: Dwight seats Hidetoshi and immediately offers to translate
jokes.punchline: Hidetoshi speaks perfect English; Dwight insists he doesn't know what he needs and tries to override him anyway
jokes.explanation: Good cringe moment. 'You don't know what you need' is a great line — Dwight's paternalism overriding clear evidence to the contrary. Solid character work.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head: 'Just once, I would like to be a puppet master and have nothing go wrong. Is that too much to ask?'
jokes.setup: Dwight reflects on his failed machinations
jokes.punchline: His complaint that he can never successfully manipulate people — delivered with genuine exasperation — is funny because he never stops trying
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Dwight self-pity, delivered with sincerity. 'Is that too much to ask?' as genuine frustration about failed manipulation is excellent character work. Economy is strong.

jokes.text: Michael returns dejected; the whole office immediately denies being attracted to him. Michael: 'You might all wanna be having sex with me right now and I wouldn't even know it.'
jokes.setup: Michael has returned from being rejected by Donna and questions whether he can read anyone's signals
jokes.punchline: Michael extends his signal-misreading anxiety to the whole office — maybe they all want him and he doesn't know
jokes.explanation: Good comedic extension of the episode's theme. Michael's existential crisis about signal-reading extends to universal doubt — 'maybe everyone wants me' as a logical conclusion. The chorus of 'Not at all. / Do not. / Please.' is a great ensemble punctuation.

jokes.text: Michael to the group: 'You might all wanna be having sex with me right now and I wouldn't even know it.' Multiple people: 'Not at all.' 'Do not.' 'Please.'
jokes.setup: Michael spirals into self-doubt about his ability to read signals
jokes.punchline: His concern that everyone might secretly want him — and the chorus of immediate, emphatic denials — is a great group deflation
jokes.explanation: The rapid-fire group denial is very funny — the multiple overlapping 'not at all / do not / please' responses suggest everyone has something personal to say. Michael's existential crisis pivot to narcissistic paranoia is peak character work.

jokes.text: Phyllis: 'Bob's warehouse guys flirt with me all the time. It's mostly harmless. Usually I don't let it go too far.' — delivered completely seriously
jokes.setup: The office tries to comfort Michael by sharing their own flirtation stories
jokes.punchline: 'Usually I don't let it go too far' — Phyllis implies she sometimes does, delivered with total calm and dignity
jokes.explanation: A quietly funny Phyllis moment. The implication of 'usually' is everything — she's had dalliances with Bob's warehouse guys and doesn't consider it a big deal. The prim delivery makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Meredith: 'Michael, I flirt with Oscar sometimes when I want him to do something for me.' Oscar: 'Why would you even say that? I don't find you even remotely attractive.'
jokes.setup: Meredith shares her own flirtation strategy to comfort Michael
jokes.punchline: Oscar's immediate and complete rejection — 'I don't find you even remotely attractive' — delivered with genuine affront rather than humor
jokes.explanation: Sharp exchange. Oscar's reaction isn't played for comedy — his offense is genuine — which makes it funnier. 'I don't find you even remotely attractive' is a beautifully blunt line that works because it's delivered as dignity, not cruelty.

jokes.text: Kevin's talking head: 'When I tore my scrote, I was seeing this really hot urologist about it, and thought she was into me. But now I think she was just doing a bunch of stuff to bill my HMO... She's touching around down there. It's easy to get confused.'
jokes.setup: The office shares stories of misread romantic signals to comfort Michael
jokes.punchline: 'She's touching around down there. It's easy to get confused.' — Kevin's conclusion that a urologist treating his scrote injury was flirting with him is both deeply Kevin and a surprisingly apt parallel to Michael's situation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Tore my scrote' is already a great Kevin phrase, but the logic — 'she was touching around down there... it's easy to get confused' — is both horrifying and a genuine (if absurd) parallel to Michael's situation. Kevin is sharing this in total sincerity as a comfort story. The character integration is perfect: this is exactly what Kevin would think and say.

jokes.text: Michael's circular logic: 'I felt like an idiot because I didn't realize I was being used. But most of the people in this office have been in the exact same position. And if I'm an idiot, then they're all idiots as well. And I hired them, which makes me an idiot, which I'm not. Just ask anybody out there.'
jokes.setup: Michael tries to reason his way out of feeling like an idiot
jokes.punchline: His logic loop — idiot hires idiots makes him an idiot which proves he's not an idiot — collapses perfectly, ending with 'Just ask anybody out there' as an appeal to external validation he hasn't actually sought
jokes.explanation: Great Michael logic spiral. The argument is internally consistent in structure but logically broken — and Michael doesn't notice it breaking. 'Just ask anybody out there' as the appeal to authority he hasn't consulted is a perfect deflating button. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Erin: 'Michael, I think Donna left this here. Should I put it in the lost and found for 14 days and then I can take it home?' — referring to Donna's barrette
jokes.setup: The office is consoling Michael about Donna; Erin arrives with a barrette
jokes.punchline: Erin's completely sincere question about barrette custody protocol — '14 days and then I can take it home' — reveals she has fully thought through the lost-and-found rules for personal gain
jokes.explanation: Good Erin moment. Her preoccupation with the lost-and-found rules and her plan to take the barrette home is simultaneously innocent and mercenary. The '14 days' specificity is the key detail.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I felt like an idiot because I didn't realize I was being used. But most of the people in this office have been in the exact same position. And if I'm an idiot, then they're all idiots as well. And I hired them, which makes me an idiot, which I'm not. Just ask anybody out there.'
jokes.setup: Michael tries to rationalize his embarrassment
jokes.punchline: His logic spirals: if he's an idiot, everyone is an idiot, he hired them, therefore he's an idiot, therefore he's not an idiot — the circular reasoning concludes with 'just ask anybody out there' as if external testimony will validate this
jokes.explanation: Michael's logic is internally consistent in its own broken way — the circle of idiocy arriving back at 'which I'm not' is a great structure. 'Just ask anybody out there' as a final appeal to nonexistent validators is the perfect button. Strong character integration — his defensive rationalizations are a core Michael trait.

jokes.text: Michael interprets Donna leaving her barrette as a romantic signal: 'People don't just take barrettes off.' Oscar: 'Michael... She doesn't want you to return the barrette. She's not interested in you.' — the whole office's defeated delivery
jokes.setup: Michael convinces himself the forgotten barrette is a deliberate come-hither signal
jokes.punchline: Oscar's flat, final 'She's not interested in you' — said gently but completely — captures the exhaustion of everyone around Michael
jokes.explanation: Good ensemble cringe moment. The comedy is in everyone's tired certainty vs. Michael's desperate hope. Oscar's 'It's not even a coincidence. It's just something that happened.' is the best specific line — a beautiful deflation of Michael's magical thinking.

jokes.text: Michael returns triumphant: 'I kissed. We kissed.' — describing returning the barrette. Cut to the whole office's disbelieving reaction.
jokes.setup: The office told Michael definitively not to go. He went anyway.
jokes.punchline: Michael actually did kiss Donna — and can't quite believe it himself — leading to a fragmented, disbelieving account. 'We did. Okay. We did. We did.'
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the episode's A-plot. Michael's fragmented account ('We ki... We did. Okay. We did. We did.') is funny because his disbelief mirrors the audience's. The episode earns this beat by setting up Donna's genuine interest early enough.

jokes.text: Gabe announces Kelly's full name: 'Kelly Rajanigandha Kapoor' — which is a real Indian name for a flower (tuberose), delivered with full corporate gravity
jokes.setup: Gabe formally announces the winner of the minority program
jokes.punchline: Kelly's middle name — 'Rajanigandha' — is delivered with great ceremony, and its contrast to the very American 'Kelly Kapoor' is the joke
jokes.explanation: A mild joke — the comedy relies on the contrast of the formal announcement with Kelly's otherwise very pop-culture-obsessed persona. Works better with knowledge that Rajanigandha means 'night-blooming tuberose.'

jokes.text: Gabe: 'They're going to be pretty pleased in Tallahassee that I snagged an Indian for the program. She'll be the first. The program's mostly Black. It's almost too Black. That didn't sound right.'
jokes.setup: Gabe celebrates getting an Indian applicant for Sabre
jokes.punchline: 'It's almost too Black. That didn't sound right.' — Gabe's immediate self-correction after saying something that definitely didn't sound right
jokes.explanation: Good Gabe moment. 'That didn't sound right' as the self-correction after 'almost too Black' is perfectly executed cringe — Gabe's corporate doublespeak failing him in real time. The understatement is the joke.

jokes.text: Kelly tells Ryan he can buy her old clothes. Ryan assumes she means free hand-me-downs; Kelly clarifies she means clothes she was going to give to Goodwill anyway — not gifting them to him.
jokes.setup: Kelly magnanimously offers Ryan her old clothes
jokes.punchline: She was going to give them to Goodwill — Ryan was not a primary beneficiary, just a garbage recipient — and she makes no effort to soften this
jokes.explanation: Good Kelly/Ryan moment. Kelly's casual dismissal of Ryan as a Goodwill-level beneficiary is consistent with her character. Not a standout joke but works as a character beat.

jokes.text: Kelly to Dwight: 'I'll never forget everything that you've done for me.' Dwight: 'Gosh.' Kelly: 'Because I never forget anything.'
jokes.setup: Kelly thanks Dwight warmly for his help
jokes.punchline: 'Because I never forget anything' — Kelly's 'gratitude' is immediately reframed as a threat. Her not forgetting is not a gift, it's a warning.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: warmth sets up 'I'll never forget' as a heartfelt statement — then 'Because I never forget anything' pivots it into a threat. The pause implied before it lands is key. Kelly's oblivious delivery (she doesn't know it sounds threatening) is what makes it land — the joke is in the gap between her intent and the effect. Extremely quotable. Peak Kelly.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head: 'Just once, I would like to be a puppet master and have nothing go wrong. Is that too much to ask?'
jokes.setup: Dwight's plan to control the minority program has backfired — Kelly has won
jokes.punchline: Dwight's complaint is not that manipulation is wrong, but that his manipulation keeps failing — framed as a reasonable aspiration
jokes.explanation: Great Dwight line. The complaint isn't about ethics — it's about execution. 'Is that too much to ask?' as a sincere question about puppet mastery is perfect Dwight self-pity. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Kelly: 'Will you make sure to come and visit me?' Ryan: 'I can't make it.' Kelly: 'What do you mean you can't make it? I haven't told you the dates.' Ryan: 'I'm sorry. What are the dates?' Kelly: 'No, you just said you couldn't make it and I didn't even tell you what the dates are.'
jokes.setup: Kelly asks Ryan to visit her at Yale
jokes.punchline: Ryan immediately says he can't make it before she's told him the dates — catching himself only when she calls it out
jokes.explanation: Sharp little Ryan/Kelly exchange. Ryan's preemptive 'I can't make it' — an automatic defensive reflex — is perfect character comedy. Kelly calling it out while Ryan scrambles to recover reveals the toxicity of their relationship in 15 seconds. Strong economy.

jokes.text: Kelly gets the Yale sweatshirt and does a celebratory leap/toss — throws it — Ryan catches it — 'And wait for it. Boom. Ah! I gave myself a front wedgie.'
jokes.setup: Kelly celebrates getting her Yale program sweatshirt
jokes.punchline: The athletic celebration ends with Kelly accidentally giving herself a wedgie — deflating the triumphant moment
jokes.explanation: 'Front wedgie' is a funny specific term, and Kelly's deflated celebration is a solid physical comedy moment. Not particularly original but well-executed.

jokes.text: Andy interrupts Kelly and Ryan's serious fight about the dates: 'Ah, scrote's still tender. I'm sorry.' Kelly: 'Andy, we're trying to have a private conversation.' Andy: 'I'm sorry.'
jokes.setup: Kelly and Ryan are in the middle of a genuine emotional confrontation
jokes.punchline: Andy barges into the conversation with 'scrote's still tender' as his explanation for his behavior — the total mismatch of Andy's physical complaint with the emotional scene
jokes.explanation: A callback to the scrote injury referenced earlier (Kevin's HMO story implied a context). Andy's intrusion is funny but the joke is primarily about the tonal mismatch. 'Scrote's still tender' as an explanation for general behavior is a good Andy line.

jokes.text: Ryan and Kelly's final argument: 'I'm not a liar.' 'Yes, you are.' 'No, I'm not.' 'It's — I don't always know the truth until I'm in it.' 'Are you sure?' 'No.'
jokes.setup: Ryan and Kelly fight about whether he's a liar
jokes.punchline: 'Are you sure?' 'No.' — Ryan's final admission that he doesn't know if he's sure he's not a liar, ending the episode on an unresolved, darkly comic note
jokes.explanation: Good closing beat. Ryan's 'I don't always know the truth until I'm in it' is both a genuinely Ryan-esque excuse and accidentally profound. The final 'Are you sure?' 'No.' perfectly captures their relationship — and the episode's theme of misreading signals — in two words.

tmdb_overview: Andy pulls out all the stops to give Erin a memorable Secretary's Day. Michael reluctantly takes Erin out to lunch and lets slip about Andy's relationship with Angela. Meanwhile, Oscar circulates a video he created that compares Kevin's voice to Sesame Street's Cookie Monster.
